choice.description: A pick among options, shaped like a `<select>`'s. `value` is the value of the picked option, the one value every picked option carries where the pick holds several, and the empty string where the pick is empty or its options carry different values. `options` lists each option in order, with the `value` it answers with and the `label` that names it. `disabled` is true while the user can't change the pick.

instructions.producer: Take the invoker command `--choose`, whose button's `value` is an option's value, or the empty string for the empty pick. Where `disabled` is false and exactly one option carries that value, make the pick that option, or empty it, and record it as the user's change, named by the button's words. Refuse any other request with `preventDefault()`: a value two options carry doesn't say which the user picks. Set `choice` and say `change` before the command's listener returns, and whenever else the published value changes.

file-list.description: File paths with optional Git status, opaque datum keys, and the path currently displayed by a file viewer.

measured-scalar.description: The latest scalar emitted by a repeatable measurement source. Authored lf-num text freezes the value a version states; the source snapshot records whether that measurement ran again.

text-document.description: UTF-8 text from a file or a selected line range: the text, or the text with the file's `name` where one document shows several files in turn, such as the one an editor has open, a `key` that names the file however its name changes, and an opaque `revision` naming the version of the file the text is, such as the one a save to a file the page binds names.

instructions.producer: Where the value names its file by `key`, reveal the address `<key>:<line>`, which `navigateToDatum` or a link to `#<id>:<key>:<line>` asks for: show that file with the caret at the start of its 1-based line, and `<key>` alone shows the file.

source-lines.description: The lines of a source file a widget is at, such as the ones an animation's current step runs, as line numbers in lf-code's range grammar: 1569,1571 or 1505-1507.

instructions.producer: Hold the numbers the source file gives the lines the widget is at, which are the numbers an lf-code excerpt's `lines` gives what it quotes, or null while it is at none, and say `change` each time they change. One value may name lines that several excerpts of the file quote: each marks the ones it quotes.

lf-gloss.description: A short explanation the reader can open beside a phrase without leaving its sentence.
lf-gloss.instructions: Write the phrase, then its explanation in a <span popover> after it, the last thing in the gloss: the reader opens it as a card beside the phrase, and print sets it after the phrase as a parenthetical note. Write a self-contained explanation at the first useful occurrence rather than on every repetition, and keep the phrase out of authored parentheses.
lf-gloss.example: Deploy through a walking skeletonA thin, end-to-end path through the real system. before parallelizing.

lf-num.description: A measured number in prose, tied to the data run that produced it.
lf-num.instructions:
Write the value with its unit as the element's text, with `source` naming the feed that measures it. Write that element into the page before calling `leaf data set`, then set `run` to the returned receipt. Add `via` when the source id doesn't say which command or query produced it.

The value stays as you wrote it. Any later write to the source, even of the same value, makes `page check` advise that the number needs another look. Use one source id per measurement.
lf-num.example: The import now takes <lf-num source="import-latency" run="a41f103e236c985b" via="uv run bench-import">184 ms</lf-num> at p95.

lf-text-document.description: Text written in the page, or from page data or a widget output, with numbered lines, syntax coloring, and an optional Markdown or HTML preview.
lf-text-document.instructions:
Write text that belongs to this version of the page, such as a passage you quote, in the `<pre>`, HTML-escaped (& before < and >), and name where it comes from with `label`. HTML drops a newline right after `<pre>`, but not after a `<code>` inside it; every other character is part of the text. For text that changes apart from the page, bind `source` to the page's data source, a file the page binds with `leaf file bind` among them, or `for` to a widget holding a `text-document` output, such as the file's editor beside it, leave out the `<pre>`, and name the file with `label` unless the value names it, as a bound file's and an editor's do. A bound file shows each write to it, whoever makes it. Set `preview` to `markdown` or `html` to add Preview and Source tabs over the same text. A Markdown preview draws the file's HTML as its author wrote it, with its script taken out, and of a file the page binds, as a bound file's value and an editor's name it by `key`, loads the pictures and files it names beside it. A `language-…` class colors the source: on a `<code>` around the text in the `<pre>`, as on any code block, or on the element itself when it has no `<pre>`. The preview's language is the default. An HTML preview is a separate document that inherits no Leaf styles, and comments can't reach inside it, so the user comments on the source. A document takes its text's height up to `--lf-bound`, 28rem by default, and scrolls inside that box past it, with a press under the box that shows the whole document. A preview's Source tab takes the preview's height. Set `--lf-bound` in lines with `lh`, as `--lf-bound: 20lh`, or to `none` to show the document whole. An HTML preview's frame always takes the bound's height, so give it a length. A document written `data-bound="end"`, such as a log, keeps a box that tall, with no press, and follows its newest line. As a workspace pane's body, any document fills the pane and scrolls inside it. To start it collapsed, put it inside `details`.

## Refreshing a source

A Markdown file bound to a source:

```html
<lf-text-document
  id="skill-source"
  source="leaf-skill"
  label="SKILL.md"
  preview="markdown"
></lf-text-document>
```

Set the source to one JSON string. For a whole file:

```bash
jq -Rs . SKILL.md | leaf data set <page> leaf-skill
```

For a selected line range instead:

```bash
sed -n '71,102p' SKILL.md | jq -Rs . | leaf data set <page> leaf-skill
```

Run the pipeline again to refresh the open page. `references/authoring-evidence.md`,
"Source files and media", owns when evidence follows a source and when it keeps a snapshot.
lf-text-document.example: **Fixed** a crash when `--config` names a missing file.

lf-toc.description: An outline of the document’s h2–h6 headings for navigating its sections and showing the reader’s position.
lf-toc.instructions: Write it empty with a stable id. It outlines the nearest tab or part containing it, or the whole main when outside those views. Add `open` to show its compact inline links on arrival; the reader can still collapse them. Set `max-level` to leave out deeper headings that are local detail; by default it lists h2 to h6.
lf-toc.example:
Migration plan

Prepare

Take a snapshot.

Check capacity

Leave headroom for the copy.

Move

Shift one cohort at a time.

lf-activity.description: A newest-first feed of the page’s comments, actions, reports, and published revisions.
lf-activity.instructions: Write it empty with a stable id.

lf-group.description: A named group of what it holds: one part of the page, named by its `label`. A widget that asks inside it takes the innermost group as its question.
lf-group.instructions: Group what belongs together under a name. `label` names the group wherever Leaf names it, such as On Me, a link to it or a thread on it. The group draws none of it: give the group the heading the page needs inside it, as for any other part of the page. A widget that asks the user, such as `lf-options`, stands in the group whose label asks its question, with the premise and evidence the answer rests on (`references/authoring-on-me.md`, "On the page"); the innermost group round it is its question. A group asks nothing itself, and one holding no question is a named part of the page like any other.
lf-group.example:
Which cache should the importer use?

Both hold a day of results; only Redis survives a restart.

In memory Nothing new to run. Redis One more service, and no cold start after a deploy.

lf-options.description: Alternatives the user can choose individually or as a set to answer a question.
lf-options.instructions: An `lf-options` asks with no attribute, and On Me holds it until the user picks. Put it in the `lf-group` whose label asks its question, with the shared premises and evidence (`references/authoring-on-me.md`, "On the page"), and each alternative's own case and picture inside its lf-option. `multiple` lets the user pick several options as one answer (references/authoring-on-me.md says when). Option cards read down the list, each as wide as the `lf-options`. `across` on the `lf-options` sets them side by side, which suits options where what the user compares, each option's picture or the evidence above the list, still reads at a card's share of the row, and the question then fits the window. Cards set across share the `lf-options`' width, and a card of a title and a sentence reads at about 18rem, so give the `lf-options` the width its cards need: the column holds two, `data-width="wide"` three, and `available` four or more, or cards that hold pictures. Keep them reading down where that share would shrink the pictures below the size at which their difference reads. The built-in Another option field takes unlisted answers, so add no catch-all option; `closed` leaves it out where only the listed options can answer, such as a page that draws its own choice, and the user can still say more in a comment. Use `for` only to point at sections or work items that exist apart from the question. A `multiple` `lf-options` needs the user's Done even when `selected` is authored. When taking in an answer in a stamped version, write `selected` on exactly the picked `lf-option` elements you authored. Leave an option the user added out of the markup; the log keeps it. Once you have finished applying the decision, give the `lf-options` `settled`, which records it: it stops asking and collapses to the pick while keeping its options and anchors.
lf-options.example:
Where should run status appear?

Both choices preserve the existing run detail.

effort: low risk: med Status on the run list One join; failures are visible without a click. effort: none risk: low Leave the list alone No work; failures stay one click away.

lf-option.description: One alternative in a decision: a compact label, or a card showing what choosing it gives the user.
lf-option.instructions: Word, label and illustrate the alternatives as `references/authoring-on-me.md` says. A card's `label` is its name wherever Leaf names it, such as On Me, and the card draws none of it: show its title in its own HTML, a leading `<strong>`. Write in the option any consequence the title or chips leave unstated, with pictures in block HTML, such as `svg.lf-drawing`. A `.lf-facts` list as a direct child of a card with a `label` floats right as a narrow column where the option is wide enough, so the options' figures line up. A compact option has no `label`: its words are its label. Mark the option you advise `recommended`, which draws its badge. Give your reason for the recommendation in prose beside the options, such as the question's paragraph, so each card states only what choosing it does. `selected` records the user's pick. Use `$restated` to withdraw that pick and ask again. A `for` target must stay useful whatever is decided, and does not supply the option's words. `value` names what the option answers wherever a view shows the options' answer, such as a board column, and the option answers with its id where it has none (read the `lf-board` instructions for the composition).

lf-code.description: A source-code excerpt with syntax coloring, highlighted lines, line-anchored remarks, and a mark on the lines another widget is at.
lf-code.instructions: Write the exact code inside pre at column 0, HTML-escaping & before < and >. Name source code's language as on any code block, with `<code class="language-python">` around the code inside pre, and leave plain transcripts or command output without one. For excerpts, set lines to the ascending source ranges quoted, such as 1505-1507,1520-1527; hi and lf-note at then use those source numbers. A note addressed to an omitted line captions the elided row. To mark the lines another widget is at, such as the code an animation's step runs, set for to the id of a widget holding a `source-lines` output: the block marks the lines it quotes, and where its pane scrolls, brings them into view there without moving the page. Several excerpts of one file can follow one widget.
lf-code.example:
def bracket(temp):
    if temp < 0:
        return "steel"
    return "cedar"
Freezing is the only threshold that matters.

lf-note.description: A prose remark anchored to a line or omitted range of its lf-code parent.
lf-note.instructions: Set at to the line number as the parent numbers it: 1-based by default, or the source number declared in lines. The note stands under that line, so a note about a key, field or definition names the line it starts on.

lf-chart.description: An Observable Plot chart authored with Plot’s API and sized to its place in the page.
lf-chart.instructions: Inside a `<pre>`, write a JavaScript expression for the options object you would pass to `Plot.plot`, HTML-escaping & before < and >. `Plot` and `width` are the names in scope, and the data goes inline. The chart requires an `ariaLabel` describing it. Leave `width` and `height` out of the options: read `width` to fit the ticks to the room, and set a height other than the default with `data-height` on the element. Write dates as ISO strings on an explicitly typed time scale, `utc` for days and months, and give moments a time zone, such as 2026-06-01T14:00Z. Use `var(--lf-series-N)` for constant or categorical colors; a continuous color scale needs a Plot scheme. Title the chart in the heading or prose around it rather than with Plot's `title`. The reader sees each point's value by pointing at it, by focusing the chart and stepping with the arrow keys, or by holding a finger on it, on every line, area, bar, cell, dot and rect, and comments on the point they are on. A comment's anchor names that point's datum as `point:` then the mark's place among those marks and each channel's value, as in `point:0;x=2026-05-11;y=26`, so it stays on the datum while its values do. The tip names the point by where it stands and then what it measures, a line for each, its label then its value, as in "week 6" over "offline sessions 8,412". To say something else, give the mark a `title` channel, such as `title: (d) => ...` among its options: its first line replaces the place and the rest the value. To show values on only some marks, or on a rule or text, give those marks Plot's `tip` option, and the others show none. The tip says the channels Plot's own tip would, those Plot's `channels` option adds included, and reads Plot's tip options: `format` to word a channel, leave it out or bring back one Plot's tip leaves out, and `pointer`, `maxRadius`, `px` and `py` for what the pointer picks. Leaf draws the tip, so leave out Plot's `tip` mark and `pointer` transforms. When `page check --render` reports overlapping labels, use fewer category ticks, choose them by `width`, or give the axis label more margin. Plot takes a mark's `dx`, `dy` and `textAnchor` as one value for the whole mark, so labels that each need their own offset, such as line ends that meet, each take a mark of their own.
lf-chart.example:
{
  ariaLabel: "Hours to first review by week: backend fell from 31 to 12, frontend from 18 to 11",
  x: {type: "utc", ticks: "monday", label: null},
  y: {grid: true, label: "hours to first review"},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["var(--lf-series-1)", "var(--lf-series-2)"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(
      [
        {week: "2026-05-04", team: "backend", hours: 31},
        {week: "2026-05-11", team: "backend", hours: 26},
        {week: "2026-05-18", team: "backend", hours: 12},
        {week: "2026-05-04", team: "frontend", hours: 18},
        {week: "2026-05-11", team: "frontend", hours: 21},
        {week: "2026-05-18", team: "frontend", hours: 11},
      ],
      {x: "week", y: "hours", stroke: "team", marker: true},
    ),
  ],
}

lf-shot.description: A before-and-after pair of screenshots with paired, slider and pixel-difference views, change outlines and scale controls.
lf-shot.instructions:
Use it for two versions of an interface. Set `before` and `after` to the paths `leaf page media` prints, and describe the pair in `alt`. `references/authoring-evidence.md` covers capture preparation, laying out captures that vary along more than one axis in a table, and registering media. Put explanation in the prose around the pair, not inside the element. When a decision turns on the change, put the pair inside the option that proposes it, or, for an accept-or-reject decision, in the question's group outside the options, where it shows both answers.

Check the pair as it first appears: Fit
shrinks the captures to the available width and, in Slider and Pixels, to the screen's
height, so a long full-page capture shows small. Open the pair on the change, or give it
page space, so the change reads there without the reader zooming first.

To open a pair on its change, set `focus-x`, `focus-y`, `focus-width` and
`focus-height` to the region it sits in, inside both captures, in their CSS pixels
from the top-left corner, with enough context around it to show what moved. Every view then
shows that region, at most at the size it had in the browser, and **Full frame** in
the **…** menu shows the rest. Set `density` to the device pixel ratio the captures
were taken at, such as `2`, whenever it isn't 1, so the focus is read in CSS pixels
and 100% shows each capture at the size it had in the browser.

Set `view` to the view that shows what the reader needs to see, since the pair opens
in it. `slider` overlays the captures in one frame, split by a divider that starts
halfway across it, and a click flips between them, so a change within an
unchanged layout, such as a color, a spacing or an element nudged a few pixels, stands
out as the frame flips. A change in one half of the frame shows one version until the
reader clicks, so set a focus centered on the change to put the divider across it.
`pair` shows each version whole, side by side or stacked, for content added, removed
or rearranged, where a flip would move everything after the change. `pixels` paints
every changed pixel, to locate changes scattered through a large frame or to show that
nothing changed outside the intended region. Without `view`, a pair opens in Slider. **Slider**, **Pair** and **Pixels**
sit in the shared header. Before and After label the header, or each frame when stacked. Pair keeps
the captures at the same scale; clicking either image opens its original. Fit places them beside one another or stacks
them, whichever draws them larger, so short wide captures stack and tall narrow ones sit
side by side; stacked frames fit together within the screen or the comparison's height limit. At 100%, both panes stay visible and scrolling either image moves
the other to the same location. The **…** menu offers Fit, 100%, Outline changes, the
Changed pixels color key and, for a pair with a focus, Full frame.

In Slider, click or tap the image to alternate between the complete Before and After
frames. Drag the divider for an intermediate comparison, or focus it and use the
arrow keys; Home and End show the complete frames.

**Outline changes** marks changed regions in Pair and Slider, using the accent color
for content that only moved. **Pixels** paints changed pixels amber over the greyed after image, softly for
small changes and more strongly for large ones, so build no difference image of your
own. It locates differences without inferring what was added or removed. Outlines and scale belong to the reader; author the pair with `before`, `after`, `alt`,
the captures' `density`, the opening `view` and, where it matters, a focus.

The comparison reports identical images, slight changes or changes throughout the
frame. If it reports identical images, or no outline sits where the prose puts the
change, capture a case that shows the change or say that nothing changed. Name subtle
changes in the prose. Where live data changed between captures, say where to look.
lf-shot.example:
The option cards

The chips now sit above the title, so a scanning eye reads cost before prose.

lf-board.description: Cards grouped into columns for scanning work and status, with movement and reordering available.
lf-board.instructions:
Use a board to show grouped work and status. When the user must make decisions, give them explicit controls or `lf-options` rather than relying on moving cards. When revising, place each card in the column and rank `state` gives it (`$verbs` defines ranks), unless the revision retracts that move by marking the card, not the board, `restated` (`authoring-revisions.md`, "Honor user state"). ## One answer in its question and on a board For this composition, read the `lf-options` and `lf-option` instructions too. When the user answers proposals beside their cases and also needs every answer in one view to compare or rearrange, keep each answer in its question's `lf-options` and add a board whose cards show those answers, rather than asking twice. Give each option a `value` naming the answer it gives, in words every question shares, and the board one column per value with that `value`, plus one column without a value for proposals not yet answered or answered in the user's own words. An option without a `value` answers with its id, which no other question shares. Each card's `shows` names its question's `lf-options`, and the card appears in the column matching that pick's value: ```html

Keep the rail?

…the case for the rail…

Next Later Keep the rail ``` A drop on the board answers through the `lf-options`, so the page holds one answer, which Undo and `restated` take back in both views. Options of one question may share a `value`: a pick of any of them puts the card in that value's column. The user can't move the card into that column on the board, since a drop wouldn't say which option they pick; they pick in the question. When a revision writes the user's pick into the `lf-options`, move the card to that pick's column too. The user can't reorder a card that shows an answer within its column; where the order within a column is itself the user's call, ask for it as its own question.
lf-board.example: Heated perch Wire the south feeder. Squirrel baffle Camera mount

lf-column.description: One named board column, including empty columns the user can move a card into.
lf-column.instructions: Write a label that names the column on its own. Use tone when landing here carries a status judgment, such as blocked, needing review, or done; otherwise leave it neutral. On a board whose cards show answers, `value` names the answer the column holds, an option's `value` or, for an option without one, its id; a column without a `value` holds the answers no column names.

lf-card.description: One board card whose identity and comments survive user moves.
lf-card.instructions: Give the card its name in `label`, which names it wherever Leaf does, such as when the user moves it, and its title and prose as content, the title a leading `<strong>`: the card draws none of its label. Keep its id stable across moves. Use `$restated` to withdraw the user's moves. `shows` makes the card a view of a decision widget's answer: it stands in the column whose `value` that answer names, and moving it changes the answer (read the `lf-board` instructions for the composition). Name a widget in the card's own page or message that holds its pick as a `choice`, as an `lf-options` does; `page check`, and the check of a message that holds the card, refuse any other.

lf-tabs.description: Several views shown one at a time: page navigation, a tabbed box, or a queue beside its open item.
lf-tabs.instructions: The first `lf-tabs` written directly in `main` owns the page's view history and URL. Give a set `flow="page"` to share the document's space without a frame, as page-layout.md describes; omit it for a boxed tab set. Visual flow does not choose history ownership. Put the page's title and lede before page tabs, and the main current view first. Make each `lf-tab` a self-contained view; history, threads and versions belong to the whole page. When current work no longer needs a view, remove it. Move any context still needed, and any passage an open thread or an unretracted decision is anchored to, into a `details` in the relevant tab. Use `list="side"` for a queue listed beside the item it opens.
lf-tabs.example:
Wire the first site this week.

Keep the original outcome and constraints in reach.

lf-tally.description: A count of the open obligations in one region, such as the decisions left in a queue, split into those waiting on the user and those waiting on the agent, with an optional control that goes to the next one waiting on the user.
lf-tally.instructions: Write it empty with a stable id, and set `for` to the region whose obligations it counts, such as a side-list `lf-tabs` queue. Place it where the reader looks for the queue's state, such as a workspace header beside its `.lf-tag` chips. Add `next` for a Next On Me control that steps through the obligations waiting on the user.
lf-tally.example:
Release triage

Ship the retry cap?

Ship the retry cap Canary the retry cap first

Remove the flag?

Remove the stale flag Keep the flag for another release

lf-tab.description: One labeled view in a tab set, optionally summarized and grouped in a side-list queue.
lf-tab.instructions: In a side-list queue, write each tab's `summary` and `group` as `page-layout.md`, "A workspace", says. Keep ids distinct across tabs, which share the page's id space.

lf-parts.description: A page made of parts, each laid out by a Layout of its own and shown one at a time, listed down the window's left edge under the page's title.
lf-parts.instructions: Place it as `page-layout.md`, "A page of parts", says, giving each `lf-part` one child carrying that part's Layout, such as `<article class="layout-column">`. Put the main current part first. History, threads and versions belong to the whole page. When current work no longer needs a part, remove it, moving any passage an open thread or an unretracted decision is anchored to into a `details` in the relevant part.
lf-parts.example:
Retry storm

Compare the two caps.

The storm started with the 2.3 release.

lf-part.description: One labeled part of a page, holding the box its own Layout arranges.
lf-part.instructions: Hold exactly one child, carrying the part's Layout. Its `summary` shows under its label in the list, so the user can tell the parts apart before opening one; start it with what the part holds unless the label already says so. Keep ids distinct across parts, which share the page's id space.

lf-draft.description: A block of text the user owns and can rewrite in place, with recorded revision history.
lf-draft.instructions:
Write the exact Markdown source as `
`, one newline, the HTML-escaped source (& before < and >), then `
` right after it. HTML drops that first newline; every later character, indentation and trailing newlines included, is part of the draft. With `required`, a draft asks the user for an edit; without it, it is an optional editing surface. Put a `required` draft in the named group of the question that asks for the edit, beside the evidence it needs (`references/authoring-on-me.md`, "On the page"). For approval of editable wording, read authoring-on-me.md, "Permission". When taking in an answer to a `required` draft in a stamped version, write the user's exact words as its body, using the `
` form above. Keep the user's exact source on revision (authoring-revisions.md, "Honor user state"); to replace an edited passage on purpose, write the new text and mark the draft `restated` ($restated).
lf-draft.example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command.

lf-sample.description: A sample: quoted content, interactive content on this page, or an isolated child Leaf page.
lf-sample.instructions: Its `label` names it wherever Leaf names it, such as a thread on it; the page doesn’t show it. Use interactive for inline controls that share this page’s state and Undo; they ask nothing, so none goes on On Me. For an isolated live child page, put its main content in one direct template[data-sample] with a stable id. Use window for a whole Leaf window including its chrome. Read live-samples.md for child-page interaction, reset, and isolation.
lf-sample.example:
I'd take the GPS, the better tool in the field.

effort: low Paper maps Nothing to charge. effort: med Dedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery.

lf-pane.description: A reading region with an optional header and footer, independently scrollable inside a full-height workspace.
lf-pane.instructions: For independent scrolling, place the pane as a full-height workspace’s body or a direct cell; elsewhere the page scrolls. Wrap multiple body blocks in one div or section. Use label to name the region accessibly and its header for the visible heading. Put action widgets in the direct footer when they should remain reachable as the body scrolls.
lf-pane.example: Read the selected record.
